candidateSources.layerA: arXiv announcement batch: Thursday 22 October 2026 (cs.AI/new, cs.CL/new, cs.MA/new — the latest batch visible as of 2026-10-23 Asia/Taipei, since arXiv does not announce on Fri/Sat/Sun). Sampled cs.AI (25/63 new submissions read), cs.MA (all 3 new submissions + 13 cross-lists), cs.CL (16/89 new submissions read). Q1-Q3 Groundlane web_search supplementary queries also run.
candidateSources.layerC: lookback from 2026-10-10 to 2026-10-22, scanned 'watch' decisions across all files; 2026-10-22 alone carried ~150 watch candidates (same-day leftovers from a large batch), all logged with credibility not-assessed by the prior run. None elevated: today's Layer A/B pool already produced three candidates with full or partial primary-source verification and strong thematic coherence (agent trust/governance over persistent state and tool actions), outscoring the decayed/unassessed Layer C pool.

candidates.title: Back Up Before You Regret: Measuring Backup Awareness and Automating Backup in Coding Agents
candidates.institution: Northeastern University + UC Berkeley + University of Chicago + UIUC
communitySignals: Third-party coverage: unite.ai article published ~4h after submission
GitHub repo + HuggingFace dataset + project page + demo video
credibilityEvidence: S3 RegretBench construction (205 tasks from X.com/GitHub/StackOverflow regret moments)
S4 Main Results across 6 frontier models (86.1% completion, 15.2% backup rate)
S5 BackUpper method + S5.2/5.3 method evaluation, efficiency, generalization, ablations
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Benchmark + multi-model evaluation + method efficiency/generalization/personalization ablations in body and appendix, though limited to a single 205-task benchmark
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Core numbers supported by multi-model benchmark plus independent efficiency/generalization experiments; already drew independent press coverage
candidates.primaryLimitation: 205 tasks drawn entirely from publicly reported regret moments, which may carry selection bias toward dramatic/memorable cases
candidates.presentationReason: Method, benchmark construction, and limitations clearly laid out with appendix detail
candidates.reason: Selected: directly measures a concrete, underexplored agent-safety gap (backup awareness) with a reproducible benchmark and a deployable, harness-agnostic fix; strongest reproducibility signal of today's pool.

candidates.title: AgentPolicyForge: From Executable Environments to Policy Benchmarks and Adaptive Guards
candidates.citationVelocity: Semantic Scholar query rate-limited (429) after repeated attempts
communitySignals: No independent GitHub/PyPI/press found in search
credibilityEvidence: S2-S3 PolicyGym construction (698 training scenarios, 254 held-out human-reviewed test scenarios across 10 policy families)
S4.2-4.5 experiments: policy-prompting baseline, trained guard, fixed vs updating archive ablation, external validation on VIOLA and PolicyGuardBench, smaller-backbone (Qwen3-8B) replication
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Multiple ablations (archive update, verifier-derived labels, smaller backbone) plus two external benchmark cross-checks (VIOLA, PolicyGuardBench) support the core claim
reproducibilityEvidence: PolicyGym construction and splits detailed in paper appendix; no public code/dataset link found at time of review
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: 40-44% relative ASR reduction is supported by paired ablations and external benchmark validation, not a single isolated number
candidates.primaryLimitation: Core evaluation is concentrated on the authors' own PolicyGym scenarios; generalization to real enterprise policy sets beyond VIOLA/PolicyGuardBench cross-checks is less established
candidates.presentationReason: Framework, benchmark construction and experiment sections are clearly separated with explicit ablation questions
candidates.reason: Selected: tackles the common and hard-to-catch case of policy-violating-but-tool-permitted calls with a trained, measurable guard rather than relying on prompt-level policy; complements BackUpper's 'preserve state' angle with 'prevent disallowed state changes'.

candidates.title: PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust
candidates.institution: AWS AI Labs (shared authors Wanyu Du, Sandesh Swamy with AgentPolicyForge; author emails match AWS AI Labs pattern)
communitySignals: No independent GitHub/PyPI/press found in search
credibilityEvidence: Abstract only: full HTML and PDF both exceeded the research tool's upstream byte limit (large embedded figures/Lean4 artifacts) and could not be fetched this round; abstract makes specific, falsifiable claims (two integrity theorems machine-checked in Lean 4, zero attack success on Trojan Hippo, up to 90-agent simulation on tau^2-bench) but body method/experiment/limitation sections were not independently read
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Abstract-level claims are specific and the formal-verification claim (Lean 4) is inherently hard to fabricate, but full experimental setup, ablations and author-stated limitations could not be verified this round
reproducibilityEvidence: No public code/proof-artifact link found within what was accessible
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Claim strength in the abstract is high, but editorial confidence is capped because the body text could not be read to check scope and caveats
candidates.primaryLimitation: Body text (HTML and PDF) could not be fetched within tool limits this round; article relies on abstract-level claims only and readers are told to treat this as preliminary
candidates.reason: Selected with explicit hedging per skill Step 6 point 4 (body unreadable -> conditional pass at most): completes today's cluster on agent trust over persistent state (memory poisoning/injection defense) with a formally-verified approach distinct from BackUpper (reversibility) and AgentPolicyForge (policy enforcement); language kept to '略讀/preliminary' strength throughout the article.

candidates.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild? (Agent4Sci)
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Abstract-level only; not deep-read this round
candidates.reason: Strong candidate (NeurIPS-accepted, concrete 10.4%->20.1% gain from plug-in skills) but sits on a different sub-theme (agent capability ceiling on ML-for-science) than today's chosen cluster on agent trust/governance over persistent state; not deep-read this round given time budget, so not elevated above three candidates whose bodies were already verified.

candidates.title: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses: Agentic Harness Evolution via Successive Scale Racing (SSR)
candidates.institution: Michigan State University + Snap Research (inferred from author list)
candidates.reason: Concrete numbers (pass rate 64.3%->68.3% as task pool scales 40->200, 60% fewer validation runs) but about harness-evolution scaling, a capability/efficiency sub-theme rather than today's trust/governance cluster; weaker thematic fit than the three selected.

candidates.title: D-Skill: Distilling Teacher Knowledge through Agent Skills
candidates.reason: Relevant (black-box skill distillation closing 75-95% of teacher-student gap) but about capability transfer/cost reduction, not the persistent-state trust theme; weaker fit than selected trio.

candidates.title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
candidates.reason: Mechanistic finding (text refusal doesn't transfer to tool calls, AUC 0.76-0.86) is relevant to agent safety, but is an interpretability/diagnostic result with no deployed defense, weaker practical link than AgentPolicyForge's trained guard with measured ASR reduction on the same general problem class.

candidates.title: Fig: Automated Multiagent Behavior Elicitor
candidates.reason: Multiagent behavior-elicitation testbed for research on cooperation/deception/sabotage is interesting but is an evaluation-methodology tool for eliciting behaviors, not directly about governing agent actions on persistent state; weaker fit and lower immediate practical link than selected trio.

candidates.title: Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths
candidates.reason: Test-time MPPI-style planning method on ALFWorld/ScienceWorld; capability-focused and benchmarked only on small simulated environments, weaker today-importance than the deployment-relevant trust/governance cluster chosen.

candidates.title: Inheritance as an Admission Test for LLM Prompt Merge Operators
candidates.reason: Single task (one negotiation game), single model (gemini-3.1-flash-lite), no fixed-oracle arm run — evaluation scope is narrow relative to the multi-model, multi-task benchmarks of selected candidates; conclusions risk overgeneralizing from one setting.

candidates.title: Credit Where Credit Is Due: Contrastive Attribution Topology Search for Multi-Agent Systems (CATS)
candidates.reason: Concrete numbers (BigCodeBench +5.3pp with 54% fewer tokens; excludes all adversarial agents in a HotpotQA prompt-poisoning stress test) make this a strong multi-agent-efficiency/credit-assignment candidate, but its core contribution is team topology optimization rather than governing persistent-state actions; good candidate for a future multi-agent-efficiency cluster.

candidates.title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination
candidates.institution: UNC Chapel Hill (Mohit Bansal lab, inferred)
candidates.reason: Generalizes to an unseen proprietary model family (GPT-5.4) across 5 environments, a strong coordination-capability result, but about theory-of-mind coordination rather than trust/governance over persistent state; weaker fit than selected trio.

candidates.title: Parallel AI Agent Collaboration as Graph-Structured Distributed Block Optimization
candidates.reason: Mostly a theoretical guarantee (fractional chromatic number bound); empirical validation limited to code-repair experiments and three public road-network simulations, narrower than the multi-benchmark evidence behind selected candidates.

candidates.title: Design and Tuning of Multi-Agent Systems Using Bayesian Evolutionary Optimization
candidates.reason: Only two benchmarks (BigCodeBench, TabPFN preprocessing) with modest, mixed gains (improves on several tasks, merely competitive on IID datasets); evidence base narrower than selected candidates.

candidates.title: Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures
candidates.institution: UC Santa Barbara (inferred from author list)
candidates.reason: Strong ablations (removing disciplinary diversity/private histories/adaptive allocation each clearly hurts) and a real capability win (beats GDN2 at 1.3B scale), but about multi-agent research-team design for self-improvement, a capability sub-theme distinct from today's trust/governance cluster.

candidates.title: SANE: Automated Scorer-Specific Metamorphic Testing for LLM Judges
candidates.reason: Concrete evaluation-reliability result (3.7x validated test families vs JRH baseline, Spearman rho 0.852 vs 0.100 against human-labeled FaithBench), relevant to agent-toolchain evaluation infrastructure, but about LLM-judge reliability testing rather than agent actions on persistent/shared state; weaker fit than selected trio.

candidates.title: Language Models Learn to Improve Language Models (LM2LM)
candidates.reason: Interesting recursive self-improvement result (Qwen3.8-27B outperforms GPT-6-sol given 300 in-context experimental records, at 33% lower data-generation cost), but 7 days old (submitted 2026-10-16) with meaningful decay, and sits on agent/LM self-improvement capability rather than today's persistent-state trust/governance cluster.

candidates.title: VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents
candidates.reason: Agent-generated-verifier benchmark (222 tasks, 4993 hidden tests, balanced accuracy 10.6-62.1 across 19 models) is relevant to agent-toolchain evaluation infrastructure, close to today's governance theme but about correctness verification rather than trust over persistent/shared state actions; good candidate for a future evaluation-focused digest.
